sec: Drug cholestasis, albumin kinetics and coagulation studies

items.q: Match each pattern of drug-induced cholestasis with its causative agents — 1) Bland cholestasis 2) Vanishing bile duct syndrome … A) Macrolides and Amoxiclav B) Anabolic steroids and estrogens
items.exp: Bland cholestasis is caused by steroids and estrogens; vanishing bile duct syndrome is caused by macrolides and amoxiclav. (Book p991)

items.q: Which of the following drugs is NOT listed as a cause of cholestatic hepatitis on this page?
items.exp: Allopurinol causes granulomatous hepatitis; NSAIDs, azathioprine, chlorpromazine, amoxiclav, and ACE inhibitors cause cholestatic hepatitis. (Book p991)

items.q: Which triad of drugs is listed as causes of granulomatous hepatitis?
items.exp: Granulomatous hepatitis is caused by Allopurinol, Carbamazepine, and Procainamide. (Book p991)

items.q: What are the molecular weight, daily hepatic production rate, and circulating half-life (T1/2) of human serum albumin?
opts: 69,000 Daltons; 15 g/day production; T1/2 of 14–21 days
150,000 Daltons; 50 g/day production; T1/2 of 5–7 days
35,000 Daltons; 5 g/day production; T1/2 of 1–2 days
90,000 Daltons; 30 g/day production; T1/2 of 28–35 days
items.exp: Albumin has a molecular weight of 69,000 Da, daily production of 15 g/day, and a half-life of 14–21 days. (Book p991)

items.q: What is the physiologic baseline range for circulating albumin, and what cutoff defines its clinical deficiency?
items.exp: Normal albumin is 3.5–5.5 g/dL, and hypoalbuminemia is defined as < 3 g/dL. (Book p991)

items.q: Why does a depressed serum albumin level have NO diagnostic utility in an acute liver injury setting?
opts: Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant with a long circulating half-life of 14–21 days
Albumin is rapidly secreted by the spleen during acute systemic inflammation
Acute hepatocyte necrosis paradoxically accelerates renal tubular albumin reabsorption
Albumin synthesis shifts to osteoblasts during acute hepatocellular stress
items.exp: Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant whose levels drop non-specifically in acute illness, and its long T1/2 (14–21 days) makes it insensitive to acute changes in hepatic synthesis. (Book p991)

items.q: Match each type of hypergammaglobulinemia causing Albumin/Globulin (A/G) ratio reversal with its etiology — 1) Monoclonal hypergammaglobulinemia 2) Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia … A) Autoimmune hepatitis B) Multiple myeloma and plasma cell disorders
items.exp: Monoclonal hypergammaglobulinemia occurs in multiple myeloma and plasma cell disorders; polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia occurs in autoimmune hepatitis. (Book p991)

items.q: Which of the following proteins is NOT listed as a negative acute-phase reactant (-ve APR) on this page?
items.exp: Other negative acute-phase reactants listed are AFP, transferrin, and transthyretin (and albumin); ceruloplasmin is a positive acute-phase reactant. (Book p991)

items.q: A critically ill patient in the ICU has acute jaundice, coagulopathy (INR 2.4), and suspected liver failure. Testing reveals normal D-dimer, normal FDP, normal fibrinogen (dysfibrinogenemia), and normal Factor VIII. What do these coagulation findings indicate?
opts: Acute hepatitis with fulminant hepatic failure (FHF)
items.exp: In FHF, INR and bilirubin are elevated, but D-dimer, FDP, fibrinogen, and Factor VIII remain normal, distinguishing it from DIC. (Book p991)

items.q: Match each parameter with its status in Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) versus Acute Hepatitis with Fulminant Hepatic Failure (FHF) — 1) D-dimer and FDP 2) Factor VIII … A) Markedly reduced in DIC, but normal in FHF B) Markedly elevated in DIC, but normal in FHF
items.exp: In DIC, D-dimer and FDP are markedly elevated (↑↑) and Factor VIII is consumed (↓↓); both are normal in FHF. (Book p991)

items.q: Assess the two statements on coagulation profiles: I Factor VIII is synthesized primarily by vascular endothelial cells, which explains why it is preserved in acute fulminant hepatic failure. II In disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), plasma fibrinogen is typically elevated as a protective compensatory mechanism.
items.exp: Statement I is true because endothelial Factor VIII production spares it in liver failure. Statement II is false because consumption in DIC causes fibrinogen levels to fall markedly (↓↓). (Book p991)
